content: The data provided outlines various adverse events and outcomes associated with treatments for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, specifically comparing the interventions of dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine and artemether-lumefantrine or artesunate-mefloquine. 1. Early Vomiting: Based on data from 2,695 participants across three randomized controlled trials, the baseline risk of early vomiting was 20 per 1,000. The intervention group showed an increase to 30 per 1,000, resulting in 10 additional cases per 1,000. The certainty of evidence was moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 2. Vomiting: Data from 6,761 participants in nine randomized controlled trials indicated a baseline risk of 90 per 1,000. There was no difference observed in the intervention group, with the risk remaining at 90 per 1,000. The certainty of evidence was moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 3. Nausea: WHO guidelines for malaria (updated October 16, 2023) report that nausea occurred in 20 per 1,000 individuals based on data from 4,531 participants in nine studies. The intervention group showed a reduction to 14 per 1,000, with six fewer cases per 1,000. The evidence was rated as moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 4. Diarrhea: Data from 4,889 participants in seven randomized controlled trials showed a baseline risk of 120 per 1,000. No difference was observed in the intervention group, with the risk remaining at 120 per 1,000. The certainty of evidence was moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 5. Abdominal Pain: Based on data from 911 participants in five studies, the baseline risk of abdominal pain was 190 per 1,000. The intervention group showed a reduction to 160 per 1,000, with 30 fewer cases per 1,000. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 6. Anorexia: Data from 3,834 participants in five studies indicated a baseline risk of 150 per 1,000. The intervention group showed a reduction to 140 per 1,000, with 10 fewer cases per 1,000. The certainty of evidence was moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 7. Headache: Based on data from 309 participants in two studies, the baseline risk of headache was 270 per 1,000. The intervention group showed an increase to 330 per 1,000, with 60 additional cases per 1,000. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 8. Sleeplessness: Data from 547 participants in two studies showed a baseline risk of 10 per 1,000. The intervention group showed an increase to 30 per 1,000, with 20 additional cases per 1,000. The certainty of evidence was low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 9. Dizziness: Based on data from 547 participants in two studies, the baseline risk of dizziness was 30 per 1,000. The intervention group showed an increase to 40 per 1,000, with 10 additional cases per 1,000. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 10. Sleepiness: Data from 384 participants in one study indicated no cases of sleepiness in either the baseline or intervention groups. The certainty of evidence was low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 11. Weakness: Based on data from 1,812 participants in five studies, the baseline risk of weakness was 170 per 1,000. The intervention group showed an increase to 180 per 1,000, with 10 additional cases per 1,000. The certainty of evidence was moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 12. Cough: Data from 4,342 participants in five studies showed a baseline risk of 420 per 1,000. No difference was observed in the intervention group, with the risk remaining at 420 per 1,000. The evidence was rated as moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 13. Coryza (Nasal Congestion): Based on data from 832 participants in two studies, the baseline risk of coryza was 680 per 1,000. The intervention group showed a reduction to 660 per 1,000, with 20 fewer cases per 1,000. The certainty of evidence was low due to serious imprecision. 14. Prolonged QT Interval (Adverse Event): Data from 1,548 participants in one study indicated a baseline risk of 30 per 1,000. The intervention group showed a reduction to 20 per 1,000, with 10 fewer cases per 1,000. The evidence was rated as low due to serious imprecision and risk of bias. 15. Prolonged QT Interval (Bazett Correction): Based on data from 1,548 participants in one study, the baseline risk was 70 per 1,000. The intervention group showed an increase to 90 per 1,000, with 20 additional cases per 1,000. The certainty of evidence was low due to serious imprecision and risk of bias. 16. Prolonged QT Interval (Fridericia Correction): Data from 1,548 participants in one study indicated no cases of prolonged QT interval in either the baseline or intervention groups. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 17. Pruritus (Itching): Based on data from 2,033 participants in five studies, the baseline risk of pruritus was 20 per 1,000. The intervention group showed an increase to 40 per 1,000, with 20 additional cases per 1,000. The certainty of evidence was moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 18. Facial Edema: Data from 384 participants in one study showed no significant difference in the risk of facial edema between the baseline and intervention groups. The evidence was consistent across trials but rated as low due to serious imprecision. 19. Serious Adverse Events (Including Deaths): Based on data from 3,522 participants in eight studies, the baseline risk of serious adverse events was 8 per 1,000. The intervention group showed an increase to 9 per 1,000, with one additional case per 1,000. The certainty of evidence was moderate due to serious imprecision. 20. Fatigue: Data from 872 participants in two studies indicated a baseline risk of 8 per 1,000. The intervention group showed a reduction to 3 per 1,000, with five fewer cases per 1,000. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risk of bias and indirectness. 21. Nightmares: Based on data from 220 participants in one study, the baseline risk of nightmares was 10 per 1,000. The intervention group showed a reduction to 1 per 1,000, with nine fewer cases per 1,000. The certainty of evidence was low due to serious risk of bias and indirectness. 22. Anxiety: Data from 522 participants in one study showed a baseline risk of 11 per 1,000. The intervention group showed a reduction to 1 per 1,000, with 10 fewer cases per 1,000. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risk of bias and indirectness. 23. Blurred Vision: Based on data from 464 participants in one study, the baseline risk of blurred vision was 9 per 1,000. The intervention group showed a reduction to 4 per 1,000, with five fewer cases per 1,000. The certainty of evidence was low due to serious risk of bias and indirectness. 24. Tinnitus: Data from 220 participants in one study indicated a baseline risk of 9 per 1,000. The intervention group showed a reduction to 4 per 1,000, with five fewer cases per 1,000. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risk of bias and indirectness. 25. Palpitations: Based on data from 1,175 participants in three studies, the baseline risk of palpitations was 18 per 1,000. The intervention group showed a reduction to 11 per 1,000, with seven fewer cases per 1,000. The certainty of evidence was moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 26. Dyspnea (Shortness of Breath): Data from 220 participants in one study showed a baseline risk of 9 per 1,000. The intervention group showed a reduction to 3 per 1,000, with six fewer cases per 1,000. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 27. Urticaria (Hives): Based on data from 719 participants in two studies, the baseline risk of urticaria was 2 per 1,000. The intervention group showed a reduction to 1 per 1,000, with one fewer case per 1,000. The certainty of evidence was low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 28. Rash: Data from 220 participants in one study showed no significant difference in the risk of rash between the baseline and intervention groups. The evidence was consistent across trials but rated as low due to serious imprecision. This summary provides a detailed breakdown of the adverse events and their associated risks, highlighting the limitations in evidence quality due to bias, imprecision, and indirectness.
